reason: The sources contain rich, overlapping details about the ship's flawed design, its sudden sinking on its maiden voyage, and its remarkable 1961 salvage.
story: In August 1628, the Swedish warship Vasa, the pride of King Gustavus Adolphus, set sail from Stockholm Harbor. Richly decorated and armed with 64 bronze cannons across two gundecks, she was designed to dominate the Baltic Sea. But she harbored a fatal secret: she was dangerously top-heavy. Before sailing, a stability test of thirty men running across the deck was halted because she threatened to capsize. Despite this terrifying warning, officials remained silent, terrified of the impatient king. Just twenty minutes into her maiden voyage, a light gust of wind struck her sails. The great ship heeled to port, water poured into her open lower gunports, and she plunged to the seabed in full view of thousands of horrified onlookers. Roughly thirty people perished. After 333 years preserved in the brackish Baltic waters, the Vasa was raised nearly intact in 1961, now resting as a haunting time capsule of royal hubris.
angle: A month before sailing, a stability test where 30 men ran across the deck was halted because the ship almost capsized—yet officials were too afraid of the king to stop the launch.

claims.claim: Before launching, a stability test was conducted where 30 men ran back and forth across the upper deck to make the ship roll.

evidence.quote: Thirty men ran back and forth across the upper deck to start the ship rolling, but the admiral stopped the test after they had made only three trips, as he feared the ship would capsize.
He asked a herd of 30 men to run back and forth across the deck; after just three runs, the ship began to teeter precariously.

claims.claim: The stability test was witnessed by Vice Admiral Klas Fleming.

evidence.quote: Söfring Hansson, arranged for the ship's stability to be demonstrated for Vice Admiral Fleming
The demonstration was witnessed by Vice Admiral Klas Fleming

claims.claim: The wreck of the Vasa remained at the bottom of the sea for over 300 years before being salvaged.

evidence.quote: after spending 333 years on the seabed.
where it stayed for more than 300 years before it was finally rediscovered.

claims.claim: The Vasa was built with two full-length gundecks.

evidence.quote: Vasa was an early example of a warship with two full-length gundecks
including a stack of two gundecks

claims.claim: The cold, low-oxygen water of the Baltic Sea preserved the ship from bacteria and wood-eating shipworms.

evidence.quote: The cold, oxygen-poor water of the Baltic Sea protected Vasa from the bacteria and worms
The water there is too brackish and deoxygenated to support the wood-munching shipworm Teredo navalis.

claims.claim: To prevent shrinking and cracking after recovery, the ship was sprayed with polyethylene glycol (PEG).

evidence.quote: its entire exterior was sprayed down with a waxy substance called polyethylene glycol, or PEG, to prevent it from shrinking.
the Vasa was continuously sprayed with polyethylene glycol (PEG)

claims.claim: The ship is now displayed in the Vasa Museum in Stockholm.

evidence.quote: moved permanently to the Vasa Museum in the Royal National City Park in Stockholm.
The remains of the ship can be found in Stockholm’s Vasa Museum.

disputed: Whether the ship's design was modified mid-build to add a second gundeck: S5 claims a second gundeck was added late during construction on the king's orders, whereas S1 cites modern laser measurements showing no such late structural modifications were made to the hull after the keel was laid. The script should present this cautiously, highlighting the modern forensic discovery.

The planned gun capacity: S4 states she was equipped with 64 guns, while S1 clarifies the original planned capacity was 72 guns, but 8 had not been delivered by the launch date. The script should clarify that the ship sailed with 64 cannons out of a planned 72.
